Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

BARCELONA, Spain -- Barcelona are ready for twice world player of the year Ronaldinho to move on, said club president Joan Laporta. Ronaldinho is expected to leave Barcelona this summer after struggling for form last season. Laporta told the Catalan TV3 station that the Brazilian midfielder, who struggled with injuries and poor form last season, needed new challenges in his career. "When the wheel turns, it's normal that the key figures leave," Laporta said. "I would like Ronaldinho to be given a great send-off so that he is remembered for all he has given us and that if he didn't do any more it was because the circumstances wouldn't allow it. "Last year, we thought that it might be the year to sell him, but given his enthusiasm and the appreciation that a club like Barcelona needs to have, we decided to let him stay on. Things haven't turned out the way he wanted them to." Laporta recognized that it might not be easy to sell Ronaldinho, who suffered a series of injury and fitness problems this season and made the starting line-up in only 13 of 38 league matches. Ronaldinho last played for Barcelona in the 2-1 loss at home to Villarreal on March 9, has suffered muscle pain in his right leg been out of action ever since. AC Milan showed an interest in signing him and his brother Robert De Assis said personal terms had been agreed. But the clubs failed to reach agreement over a transfer fee. After a second successive season without a trophy Barcelona announced on May 7 that Rijkaard would leave at the end of the season and be replaced by former player Josep Guardiola. "We decided that if Frank did not continue then we would choose Guardiola because Pep possessed the necessary humility," said Laporta. "We didn't think about coaches like Mourinho or (Rafa) Benitez, who are both great coaches, but aren't right for Barcelona. So we told Rijkaard that when he left Guardiola would take his place." Barca's arch-rivals Real Madrid, who lifted another Spanish title this season, have signed their first newcomer for the next campaign by paying a reported 10 million euros ($15.5 million) for Argentine defender Ezequiel Garay from Racing Santander. Marca newspaper said the 21-year-old Argentine had signed a six-year contract. Meanwhile, reports that Real could be making a move for Manchester United's Cristiano Ronaldo were dismissed by coach Bernd Schuster. "I prefer to spend my time talking about things that have some bearing to reality," he told a press conference. Marca had reported that Real were still interested in buying Ronaldo who has put off all talk of his future until after the Champions League final.

# The Fading Magic: The End of Ronaldinho's Barcelona Era

## When the Samba Stopped Dancing

There was a time when the Camp Nou would erupt into rhythmic applause not just for goals, but for moments of pure artistry that only one man could conjure. Ronaldinho, the buck-toothed magician from Porto Alegre, had transformed FC Barcelona from a slumbering giant into the most watchable team on the planet. But by the summer of 2008, the music had faded, and the club faced the painful reality that its greatest entertainer had reached the end of his remarkable journey in Catalonia.

## The Golden Years

When Ronaldinho arrived at Barcelona in 2003, the club was in crisis. Trophyless and struggling for identity, they turned to the Brazilian who had shone at Paris Saint-Germain. What followed was nothing short of a renaissance. Two consecutive La Liga titles in 2005 and 2006, culminating in the 2006 Champions League triumph in Paris, established Ronaldinho as the beating heart of a resurgent Barça.

His individual accolades matched the collective glory—back-to-back FIFA World Player of the Year awards in 2004 and 2005, and the Ballon d'Or in 2005. Perhaps his crowning moment came at the Santiago Bernabéu in November 2005, when even Real Madrid supporters rose to applaud his mesmerizing performance in a 3-0 demolition of their bitter rivals.

## The Decline Begins

But football, like all forms of magic, requires discipline to sustain. By the 2007-08 season, the warning signs that had flickered in the previous campaign became impossible to ignore.

### Injury Troubles

Ronaldinho's body began to betray him. A series of muscular problems and a persistent thigh injury limited his availability throughout the 2007-08 season. He managed only a handful of appearances as the campaign wore on, his explosive acceleration and low center of gravity—the foundations of his genius—compromised by physical setbacks.

The injuries were symptomatic of a deeper problem. Reports emerged of a lifestyle increasingly at odds with the demands of elite football. His famous love for Barcelona's nightlife, once tolerated as the eccentricity of a genius, now appeared to be undermining his conditioning and commitment.

### Poor Form

On the pitch, the decline was stark. The player who once toyed with defenders now looked ponderous. The tricks that had defined him—the elastico, the no-look passes, the impossible free-kicks—came less frequently and connected less often. His statistics told the story: a fraction of the goals and assists that had made him the league's most feared attacker just two seasons prior.

The 2007-08 season was a disaster for Barcelona as a collective. Finishing third in La Liga, a distant eighteen points behind champions Real Madrid, and suffering a Champions League semi-final exit to Manchester United, the team lacked the spark that Ronaldinho had once provided in abundance.

## The Transition Plan

The appointment of Pep Guardiola as manager in the summer of 2008 signaled a decisive break from the past. The former club captain, stepping up from the Barcelona B team, arrived with a clear vision and an uncompromising philosophy.

### A New Direction

Guardiola made his intentions clear almost immediately. He informed both Ronaldinho and Deco that they were not part of his plans for the future. The new manager sought to build his team around a young, homegrown talent named Lionel Messi—a player who had learned at Ronaldinho's side and was now ready to inherit the mantle.

The decision was as much about culture as it was about performance. Guardiola demanded total professionalism and dedication. He wanted players who would embody the values of the club, both on and off the pitch. In this new Barcelona, there was no room for the indiscipline that had crept into the squad during Ronaldinho's final season.

### The Passing of the Torch

There was a poetic quality to the transition. Messi, who had worn the number 30 and later the number 19, would eventually take Ronaldinho's iconic number 10 jersey—a symbolic passing of the torch from one Argentine-Brazilian era to the next. The young Argentine had often credited Ronaldinho for welcoming him into the first team and helping him settle, making the succession feel like a natural evolution rather than a brutal replacement.

## The Departure

In July 2008, the inevitable was confirmed. Ronaldinho joined AC Milan in a transfer worth approximately €21 million. The Brazilian, still only 28, sought to revive his career in Serie A, hoping the Italian environment would reignite the flame that had dimmed in Spain.

His departure marked the end of a five-year love affair with Barcelona—a relationship that had begun in desperation and blossomed into one of the most memorable partnerships in the club's storied history.

## Legacy

Though his final season ended in disappointment, Ronaldinho's contribution to Barcelona cannot be overstated. He arrived when the club needed hope and left having restored its winning mentality and global appeal. He built the foundation upon which Guardiola would construct one of the greatest teams in football history.

The dream team that would go on to win everything under Guardiola—including the historic sextuple in 2009—owed a debt to the Brazilian who had shown a generation what Barcelona could be. Ronaldinho didn't just play for Barcelona; he made people fall in love with the club again.

His era ended not with a trophy or a triumphant farewell, but with the quiet acknowledgment that all magic eventually fades. Yet for those who witnessed him at his peak, Ronaldinho remained the man who brought joy back to the Camp Nou—the smiling genius whose brilliance illuminated an entire era before the samba finally stopped dancing.
